newsitem.title: GERMANY: Weak point poses fresh flood threat for Germany.
newsitem.headline: Weak point poses fresh flood threat for Germany.

text.p: A new weak point emerged in dikes holding back the swollen River Oder on Friday, posing a fresh danger to the flood-threatened Oderbruch region of eastern Germany.

Soldiers and relief workers who spent the day battling to shore up sodden flood barriers near the towns of Hohenwutzen and Reitwein faced another emergency when officials reported a weakening of the dike close to the village of Zollbruecke.
"We now have to speak of three crisis points," said Matthias Platzeck, the environment minister of Brandenburg state.
Platzeck said workers were now felling trees in the area to allow helicopters to fly in and drop sand to reinforce the dike.

"We can see that this permanent water pressure is slowly making the dike sodden along the whole stretch of the river," Platzeck said, adding that the situation at Zollbruecke was not yet as serious as at the other two crisis points.

The flood waters have already claimed more than 100 lives in Poland and the Czech Republic. They have threatened the entire Oderbruch basin for more than a week, weakening the dikes to the point of collapse.

The looming failure of the most fragile dike, at Hohenwutzen, threatened to flood an area 17 km (11 miles) wide and 50 km (30 miles) long on Germany's border with Poland, submerging dozens of villages, farms and factories.
"The chances that the dike will break are more probable than that we will be able to hold it," said a spokesman for the flood crisis committee in nearby Bad Freienwalde.

European Commissioner Monika Wulf-Mathies said during a visit to the region that the EU could provide around 87 million marks ($47 million) in immediate relief for flood victims and was also considering a broader reconstruction effort.
"We want to see what we can do to stabilise the dikes and build them back up again when the water has gone and afterward get the infrastructure back up and running," she said.
"The EU would support a common programme for the Czech Republic, Poland and Germany."
Tens of thousands of people have been evacuated from the three-country region in central Europe, where floods have also destroyed homes, farms and livestock.

While there have been no flood-related deaths in Germany, damage to houses and farms has been extensive. Around 15,000 people have been evacuated from the region since last week and thousands more warned to be ready to leave their homes at a moment's notice as the likelihood of a dam break grows daily.

"I hope it holds for the next seven days," said Manfred Stolpe, premier of Germany's affected Brandenburg state, casting a nervous glance towards soldiers frantically loading sandbags to prop up the dike in Hohenwutzen, on a bend in the Oder.
Further upstream at Reitwein, cracks appeared in a 1,200 metres (0.75 mile) stretch of the dam. A dam break at the same site caused the region's last flood in 1947.
Many increasingly despondent German local officials were saying only a miracle could save the Oderbruch river plain with its 800 square km of low-lying fertile farmland.

The Polish government estimates damage from the floods could be as high as $1.4 billion, and German officials have put the cost to their country at around one billion marks ($540 million). In the Czech Republic, economists have said damage could be as high as $2.6 billion.
The floods have torn up roads and highways, contaminated water supply and power, railway and telecommunications networks. Damage to local farms has been extensive.

Oskar Lafontaine, chairman of the opposition Social Democrats, said during a visit that his party would put a motion to the Bonn parliament to request an additional 100 million marks in aid for victims.
The government has already earmarked some 200 million marks to compensate families and businesses. ($ = 1.846 German Marks)
